title: Six years
hook: years of hard austerity; some think he has died

segments.voice: Yesterday, a handful of beans: the wanderer starved to a spine like a string of beads. Your line was starving isn't holy. Did you eat one meal slowly? Day forty-six.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF BEANS — STARVING ISN'T HOLY.`

segments.voice: Think of the longest you've ever kept at something hard. A degree that took years. A job you hated but couldn't leave. Caring for someone who was ill. There's a point in any long, hard stretch when you stop being able to tell whether you're being brave or just stubborn. When pushing on and being stuck look exactly the same. Tradition says the wanderer spent six years this way, in the forests near Uruvela. Breathless meditation. Fasting. Standing in the sun. Lying on thorns, some tellings say. His five companions watching, waiting. And one day he collapses. Today, six years.
screen: `BRAVE, OR JUST STUBBORN?` → `SIX YEARS IN THE FOREST.` → `ONE DAY HE COLLAPSES.`

segments.voice: In the Buddha's own account, there's a strange moment. He says that when some gods saw him in that state, they said, the wanderer Gotama is dead. Others said, he's not dead, but he's dying. And others said, he's neither: this is simply how an awakened one lives. Nobody could tell. The later telling makes it even more vivid. He faints while walking, and falls to the ground, and a god runs to his father, King Suddhodana, with the news: your son is dead. And the old king, who had tried so hard to keep him in the palace, refuses to believe it. My son will not die, he says, before he reaches what he went looking for. Six years. Notice that the six years come from tradition; the oldest texts don't count them. But the length is the point. This wasn't a weekend. It was the best years of a young man's life, given completely to one method. And the Buddha's verdict, looking back, is calm and devastating. Whatever painful feelings any wanderer has ever felt, he says, past, present or future, this was the most. There's none beyond it. And still, it didn't lead to awakening. Harder isn't always better. That can be a hard thing to hear if you've built a life on grit. The Buddha isn't against effort. He'll later make right effort part of the path. What he's saying is that effort pointed the wrong way just digs deeper into the wrong place. Sometimes the bravest thing is to stop.
screen: `DEAD, DYING, OR AWAKE?` · `MY SON WILL NOT DIE YET.` · `THE MOST PAIN ANYONE HAS FELT.` · `EFFORT POINTED THE WRONG WAY.` · then, large: `HARDER ISN'T ALWAYS BETTER.`

segments.voice: Sit, or even lie down if you can. Let the body be heavy. Notice where you're tired: the eyes, the back, the legs, the mind. Don't fix it. Don't push through it. Just admit it, gently, to yourself: I'm tired here. On each out-breath, let that place get a little heavier, a little more supported by the chair or the floor. You're allowed to rest. The Buddha found out the hard way. The bell holds the time.
Six years. The time tradition gives to the wanderer's austerities: the most pain anyone had felt, and still not the way.
Your line: harder isn't always better. Today, when you're tired, rest for five minutes instead of pushing through, and see what the rest gives back. Day forty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhists speak of the six years of austerities as the extreme the Buddha tried and set aside, and teachers often use them to warn against both laziness and self-punishment in practice.

match.prompt: what's inside the six years — tap the pairs.
pairs: refused to believe his son was dead

myth: the oldest suttas count exactly six years of austerity
the six years come from tradition; the oldest texts don't count them.
in the Buddha's account, some gods thought he was dead
others thought he was dying, and others that he was awake.
right effort is part of the path. he rejected effort pointed the wrong way.

fork.setup: you're King Suddhodana. a messenger runs in: your son has died in the forest. what do you say?
options: send soldiers to bring the body home.
my son will not die before he finds what he's looking for.
fork.reveal: in the later telling, the old king refuses to believe it. and he's right: the wanderer had only fainted.

original.note: Pali (Sanskrit tapas): heat, austerity, the burning practice of self-denial the ascetics believed would purify.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha meditated in the forest for six years.
what it means: he spent years in extreme self-denial, and found that harder isn't always better.
what a scholar hears: MN 36 has deities disagree whether he is dead, dying or an arahant; the six-year figure and Suddhodana's refusal come from the Nidanakatha.

sources.ref: Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36): the gods' views and the verdict on austerities
Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the six years, the fainting, and King Suddhodana

notes: The six years: traditional (commentaries); MN 36 and MN 26 don't give the number. Confirm.
Lying on thorns: MN 12 lists such practices among those the Bodhisatta tried; the script says 'some tellings say'. Confirm.
MN 36 verdict paraphrased: whatever painful feelings ascetics in past, future or present have felt, this is the utmost. Confirm.
Suddhodana's refusal is paraphrased from the Nidanakatha; confirm.
